provenance.other: “search the scriptures” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 5:39, where the KJV renders the Greek as an imperative — 'Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life' — a rendering that made the phrase a nineteenth-century commonplace for private Bible study. Alma 14:1 has the phrase as a result of preaching: those who believed 'began to repent, and to search the Scriptures'.
provenance.significance: The KJV's imperative is a translator's choice and the choice is what the Book of Mormon inherits. Read as an indicative — 'ye search the scriptures' — John 5:39 is a rebuke: you comb the writings for life and refuse the one they testify of. Read as the KJV reads it, it is a command, and Alma 14:1 obeys it. The verse before this one is Alma's testimony that the scriptures testify of the Son (13:16, 13:26), which is John 5:39's second clause; so the Book of Mormon has both halves of the verse and takes the first in the KJV's sense. Ammonihah then burns the very records the converts have begun to search (14:8), which makes the borrowing structural as well as verbal.

14:1.note: 'Many of them did believe on his words, and began to repent, and to search the Scriptures.' Three words of a KJV singleton, and a singleton whose familiarity in 1830 rests entirely on the KJV's imperative rendering. Held at moderate: the phrase is short, and 'search the scriptures' had become detached devotional English long before the Book of Mormon.
14:1.whyNot: Three ordinary words. By 1830 'search the scriptures' was a slogan of the tract societies and could reach a writer with no particular verse in view.
14:1.text: Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me.

provenance.other: “put her away privily” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 1:19, and it is the KJV's only instance of the verb 'put away' governed by 'privily'. The adverb alone is common — “privily” occurs in fifteen KJV verses — but almost always of lying in wait or slandering, never of disposing of a person. Alma 14:3 reads 'they sought to put them away privily'.
provenance.significance: The senses are opposite and that is the interest of the row. Matthew 1:19 is an act of MERCY: Joseph, unwilling to make Mary a public example, resolves on a quiet divorce. Alma 14:3 is an act of murder: the men of Ammonihah, having failed to convict Alma and Amulek publicly, decide to be rid of them without a trial. The KJV idiom for sparing someone humiliation has become the idiom for a secret killing, and the pivot is the euphemism itself — 'put away' will carry either sense in English, and 'privily' is what both parties want.

14:3.note: 'Because they had testified so plainly against their wickedness, they sought to put them away privily.' Four words of a KJV singleton, in the same grammatical shape. Recorded as an echo at moderate under CONVENTIONS §0a because the rarity is absolute and the transfer is interesting; a cautious editor would file it as wrong-sense and the whyNot says why.
14:3.whyNot: The situations have nothing in common. Joseph is contemplating a merciful divorce and the men of Ammonihah are contemplating murder, and 'put away privily' is transparent enough English that a writer could assemble it without Matthew 1:19. The context score is 1 for that reason.
14:3.text: Then Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily.

provenance.other: “pains of hell” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 116:3, 'the sorrows of death compassed me, and the pains of hell gat hold upon me.' The nearest relatives use a different noun: 2 Samuel 22:6 and Psalm 18:5 both read 'the sorrows of hell compassed me about'. Alma 14:6 has the rare noun from Psalm 116 and the verb of encirclement from the other two: 'he began to be encircled about by the pains of hell.'
provenance.significance: The composite is doing something the psalm cannot. In all three psalms the pains or sorrows of hell are an external assault — death and Sheol close on a man from outside, and the psalmist is delivered from them. Alma 14:6 makes the encirclement a function of conscience: it follows immediately on 'his soul began to be harrowed up, under a consciousness of his own guilt', so what surrounds Zeezrom is his own knowledge of what his lying words did. The Book of Mormon regularly turns hell into a state rather than a place, and this verse shows the operation being performed on the KJV's own vocabulary — Psalm 116's noun inside Psalm 18's verb, with guilt supplied as the cause neither psalm names.

14:6.note: 'His soul began to be harrowed up, under a consciousness of his own guilt; yea, he began to be encircled about by the pains of hell.' A KJV singleton for the noun and the compassing verb of its two nearest parallels, fused. Zeezrom's is the fullest conversion in the chapter and it is narrated in the psalter's language of the pit. Note also 'the blindness of the minds which he had caused', which returns to the doublet adjudicated at Alma 13:4.
14:6.text: The sorrows of death compassed me, and the pains of hell gat hold upon me: I found trouble and sorrow.

provenance.route: John 9:34 with Acts 7:57-58 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “they cast him out” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Luke 20:15 (the heir thrown out of the vineyard) and John 9:34, where the man born blind is expelled by the authorities for testifying to his healing. “spit upon him” occurs in exactly four, three of them the mockery of Jesus. The accusation Zeezrom draws — 'Art thou also possessed with the Devil?' — is the crowd's charge in John 10:20, 'He hath a devil, and is mad; why hear ye him?', a phrase occurring in exactly four KJV verses, two of them in that one exchange.
provenance.significance: Zeezrom's verse runs a complete expulsion sequence: he confesses before the court, he pleads for the accused, he is charged with possession, he is spat upon, he is cast out, and men are sent to stone him. Every stage of that is a KJV scene, and the two the sequence follows most closely are the ones where a witness rather than a defendant is destroyed — John 9, where the healed man is cast out for saying who healed him, and Acts 7, where Stephen is cast out of the city and stoned. Ammonihah does to its own lawyer what the Sanhedrin did to its own witnesses. The Stephen material returns at 14:21 with a KJV singleton, which is where that row is filed.

14:7.note: 'They reviled him, saying: Art thou also possessed with the Devil? … they spit upon him, and cast him out from among them … and sent men to cast stones at them.' No single verse is reproduced; what is reproduced is a sequence, and each of its stages is one of a handful of KJV verses. Held at moderate because the case is cumulative rather than verbal — but the cumulation is tight, six stages in one verse, and the two KJV expulsions it tracks are the two where the person cast out is a witness.
14:7.text: They answered and said unto him, Thou wast altogether born in sins, and dost thou teach us? And they cast him out.

provenance.other: “cast it into the fire” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Exodus 32:24 (Aaron and the calf) and Jeremiah 36:23, which is the Bible's only scene of a written prophecy being deliberately burned: 'he cut it with the penknife, and cast it into the fire that was on the hearth, until all the roll was consumed in the fire.' Alma 14:8 has 'cast them into the fire', 14:9 has those 'consumed by fire', and 14:14 has 'the records which were cast in with them, were consumed'. The other candidate the machine ranks, John 15:6's 'cast them into the fire, and they are burned', shares five words but is a parable of fruitless branches.
provenance.significance: Jeremiah 36 is the KJV's precedent for what Ammonihah does, and the Book of Mormon has raised the stakes by one term. Jehoiakim burns the scroll; the men of Ammonihah burn the scriptures AND the people who believe them, in the same fire and in the same sentence — 'whosoever believed … they caused that they should be cast into the fire; and they also brought forth their records which contained the Holy Scriptures, and cast them into the fire also.' The equation of a book with the believers who read it is the chapter's own contribution. Jeremiah 36:32 answers the burning by having the roll rewritten with 'many like words added'; Alma 14 answers it by having the city destroyed, which is the direction Genesis 19 supplies at 14:24.

14:8.note: 'They caused that they should be cast into the fire; and they also brought forth their records which contained the Holy Scriptures, and cast them into the fire also, that they might be burned and destroyed by fire.' Catalogued as figural: the verbal contact is a two-verse phrase and the word 'consumed', and the argument is the scene. Jeremiah 36 is the one biblical burning of scripture, and the burning of a prophetic record by the authority that has just rejected its prophet is a type-scene the Book of Mormon reproduces stage for stage. Confidence moderate — the wording alone would not carry it.
14:8.whyNot: 'Cast into the fire' is ordinary English for burning and needs no source. If the Jeremiah 36 scene is declined, the verse has no biblical dependence beyond the machine's John 15:6, which is about branches.
14:8.text: And it came to pass, that when Jehudi had read three or four leaves, he cut it with the penknife, and cast it into the fire that was on the hearth, until all the roll was consumed in the fire that was on the hearth.

provenance.other: “blood crieth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 4:10, and so does the clause it belongs to, “crieth unto me from the ground”. Alma 14:11 has 'the blood of the innocent shall stand as a witness against them, yea, and cry mightily against them at the last day'. The exact string “the blood of the innocent” is in no KJV verse — the KJV's phrase is 'innocent blood', in nineteen verses — so the contact is with the crying, not with the epithet.
provenance.significance: Genesis 4:10 supplies the one thing this verse needs and no other KJV text gives it: blood that speaks. Alma is explaining why he will not put out his hand to stop the burning, and the reason is evidentiary — the martyrs' blood is being laid up as testimony for a trial. That is Abel's blood, which cries from the ground and convicts, moved forward to 'the last day'. The eschatological relocation is the Book of Mormon's, and it is the same move Revelation 6:10 makes with the same image, where the souls of the slain cry 'How long, O Lord … dost thou not judge and avenge our blood'. Alma 14:26 will quote that verse's first four words exactly, which is why this row and that one belong together.

14:11.note: 'The blood of the innocent shall stand as a witness against them, yea, and cry mightily against them at the last day.' The verbal contact is one word — the blood cries — but that word is a KJV singleton's whole point and there is nowhere else in the Bible to get it. Held at moderate because a phrase this compressed could be reached through the general currency of Abel's blood rather than through Genesis 4:10 itself.
14:11.text: And he said, What hast thou done? the voice of thy brother’s blood crieth unto me from the ground.

provenance.other: “lake of fire and brimstone” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 20:10; the neighbouring formulations differ — 19:20 has 'a lake of fire burning with brimstone' and 21:8 'the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone'. Alma 14:14 has the 20:10 form exactly: 'that they shall be cast into a lake of fire and brimstone'.
provenance.significance: The judge's sentence is the chapter's cruellest joke and it turns on this borrowing. He has just watched women and children burn, he strikes the preachers on the cheek, and what he mocks them for is preaching a lake of fire — 'After what ye have seen, will ye preach again unto this people, that they shall be cast into a lake of fire and brimstone?' The verse he is mocking is Revelation 20:10, where the lake of fire is where the DEVIL is cast, and Revelation 21:8, where it is the portion of murderers. Ammonihah has performed the punishment it denies. The Book of Mormon does not point this out; the borrowed phrase does it, which is metalepsis working exactly as Hays describes.

14:14.note: 'Will ye preach again unto this people, that they shall be cast into a lake of fire and brimstone?' A six-word KJV singleton in the mouth of the man who has just burned people alive. The n-gram stream proposed both Revelation 19:20 and 20:10; the wording is 20:10's.
14:14.text: And the devil that deceived them was cast into the lake of fire and brimstone, where the beast and the false prophet are, and shall be tormented day and night for ever and ever.

provenance.route: 1 Kings 22:24-27 (= 2 Chronicles 18:23-26) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “smote Micaiah on the cheek” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Kings 22:24, and its chronicler's parallel at 2 Chronicles 18:23 has the preposition Alma uses, 'smote Micaiah upon the cheek'. “upon the cheek” occurs in exactly four KJV verses (2 Chronicles 18:23, Job 16:10, Psalm 3:7, Micah 5:1). The New Testament's passion strikes are worded otherwise — Matthew 26:67 'smote him with the palms of their hands', John 18:22 'struck Jesus with the palm of his hand' — so a cheek-blow delivered to a prophet with a taunt attached is Micaiah's scene, not Jesus's.
provenance.significance: 1 Kings 22 is the Bible's one full narrative of a prophet struck on the cheek and then jailed for his prophecy, and Alma 14:14-22 reproduces its sequence: the blow, the taunt ('Which way went the Spirit of the LORD from me to speak unto thee?' answered by 'After what ye have seen, will ye preach again unto this people?'), the committal to prison, and the deliberate deprivation of food and water — 1 Kings 22:27's 'feed him with bread of affliction and with water of affliction' becomes Alma 14:22's withholding of both. Micah 5:1 supplies the inversion that makes the Book of Mormon's version sharper: there it is 'the JUDGE of Israel' who is smitten upon the cheek, and here it is the chief judge who does the smiting.

14:14.note: 'He smote them with his hand upon their cheeks, and saith unto them, After what ye have seen, will ye preach again unto this people?' The single KJV verse where a prophet is smitten on the cheek by a hostile official is 1 Kings 22:24, and the preposition Alma uses is the chronicler's at 2 Chronicles 18:23. Catalogued as an allusion at moderate: the shared wording is three words, and the case rests on the four-stage sequence set out in provenance. The blow is repeated at 14:15, 14:20 and 14:24, which the recurrence list records.
14:14.whyNot: Three words, and men have always struck prisoners on the face. If the reader declines the Micaiah sequence, nothing verbal remains but 'upon the cheek', which four KJV verses share.
14:14.text: But Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah went near, and smote Micaiah on the cheek, and said, Which way went the Spirit of the LORD from me to speak unto thee?

provenance.route: Matthew 27:12 / Mark 15:3-5 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “answered nothing” occurs in exactly five KJV verses. One is 1 Kings 11:22, where it is not a silence at all but Hadad's reply 'Nothing'. The other four are the same silence in the same trial: Matthew 27:12 before Pilate, Mark 14:61 before the high priest, Mark 15:3 and 15:5 before Pilate again. There is no other silent defendant in the KJV.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon repeats the phrase three times in three verses — 'answered him nothing' (14:17), 'they answered them nothing' (14:18), 'they answered nothing' (14:19) — which is the frequency the passion narrative itself uses, and in the same escalating order: silence before the court, silence before the visiting delegation, silence when commanded to speak. Mark 15:5 supplies the reaction as well, 'so that Pilate marvelled'; Alma 14:19's judge does not marvel but commands, and the command fails. The silence is what makes the Pilate question at 14:19 land, and that verse's row records the other half.

14:17.note: 'Alma and Amulek answered him nothing; and he smote them again, and delivered them to the officers to be cast into prison.' Two words, but two words that in the KJV describe one man on one day. Held at moderate on the wording alone; the triple repetition across 14:17-19 and the Pilate question that follows are what make the case, and they are catalogued at the verses where they fall.
14:17.text: And when he was accused of the chief priests and elders, he answered nothing.

provenance.other: “I have power to” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 10:18 (Jesus of laying down his life) and John 19:10, Pilate's 'knowest thou not that I have power to crucify thee, and have power to release thee?' Alma 14:19 is 'Know ye not that I have power to deliver ye up unto the flames?' — the same interrogative frame, the same verb of possessing power, and the same substitution of the local method of execution for the word 'crucify'.
provenance.significance: The scene is built to make the borrowing work. John 19:9-10 has Jesus refusing to answer Pilate, and Pilate reacting to the silence with the claim of power; Alma 14:17-19 has Alma and Amulek refusing to answer, three times, and the judge reacting with the same claim in the same grammar. Recover John 19:11 and the reply the Book of Mormon leaves unspoken is there: 'Thou couldest have no power at all against me, except it were given thee from above.' Alma has already given that answer, at 14:11 — 'he doth suffer that they may do this thing … that the judgments which he shall exercise upon them in his wrath, may be just.' The chapter puts Pilate's question and John's answer eight verses apart and never names either.

14:19.note: 'Why do ye not answer the words of this people? Know ye not that I have power to deliver ye up unto the flames? And he commanded them to speak; but they answered nothing.' Six words in the frame of one of two KJV verses, and the other of the two is not an accusation. The n-gram stream ranked John 19:10 first here and was right; what reading supplies is the answer at John 19:11, which the Book of Mormon has already given at 14:11.
14:19.text: Then saith Pilate unto him, Speakest thou not unto me? knowest thou not that I have power to crucify thee, and have power to release thee?

provenance.other: “gnashed on him with their teeth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 7:54. The distinction matters because the KJV's other gnashing is a different idiom entirely: 'gnashing of teeth' occurs in seven verses, all of them the formula 'weeping and gnashing of teeth' for the torment of the damned, and none of them an act performed BY a mob UPON a person. Alma 14:21 has the Acts idiom — 'gnashing their teeth upon them, and spitting upon them'.
provenance.significance: Stephen's death is the New Testament's model martyrdom and Alma 14 has taken it in two pieces. The gnashing is here; the rest was at 14:7, where those who believed are cast out and men are sent to cast stones at them — Acts 7:58's 'cast him out of the city, and stoned him'. What the Book of Mormon adds is the taunt, 'How shall we look when we are damned?', and the addition is where the two gnashings meet: the men of Ammonihah gnash their teeth in the manner of Acts 7:54, and the phrase 'gnashing of teeth' everywhere else in the KJV names what will be done to them for it. They are quoting their own sentence and they know it, which is why the sentence is a question.

14:21.note: 'Many such things did they say unto them, gnashing their teeth upon them, and spitting upon them, and saying, How shall we look when we are damned?' A five-word KJV singleton, and the singleton is the one place in the Bible where gnashing is an assault rather than a torment. With the stoning at 14:7, Ammonihah's treatment of the believers is Stephen's death distributed across the chapter.
14:21.text: When they heard these things, they were cut to the heart, and they gnashed on him with their teeth.

provenance.other: “hunger and thirst and are naked” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 4:11 — 'Even unto this present hour we both hunger, and thirst, and are naked, and are buffeted, and have no certain dwellingplace.' “are naked” occurs in exactly two, that verse and Hebrews 4:13, where the sense is 'laid open'. Alma 14:22 has all three of Paul's terms in Paul's order: 'they did withhold food from them, that they might HUNGER, and water, that they might THIRST; and they also did take from them their clothes, that they were NAKED'.
provenance.significance: Paul's triad is a list of what happens to apostles, and its point is that the Corinthians are full while the apostles starve. Alma 14:22 converts each item from a condition into a deliberate act, and states the intention every time: not that they hungered, but that food was withheld SO THAT they might hunger. The same three deprivations, three times attributed to a will. Behind it stands 1 Kings 22:27, where Micaiah is to be fed 'bread of affliction and water of affliction' until the king returns in peace — the Old Testament scene the chapter has been tracking since the blow on the cheek at 14:14 — and Ammonihah improves on Ahab by withholding both.

14:22.note: 'They did withhold food from them, that they might hunger, and water, that they might thirst; and they also did take from them their clothes, that they were naked.' Paul's three-term list of apostolic destitution, in his order, from a KJV singleton, with each term turned into a purpose clause. The machine proposed Genesis 3:7 here on 'that they were naked', which is the wrong nakedness; the exclusion register carries it.
14:22.text: Even unto this present hour we both hunger, and thirst, and are naked, and are buffeted, and have no certain dwellingplace;

provenance.other: “and we will believe him” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 27:42, the chief priests at the cross: 'He saved others; himself he cannot save. If he be the King of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him.' “come down from the cross” occurs in exactly three (Matthew 27:40, 27:42, Mark 15:30). Alma 14:24 has the conditional, the demand for self-deliverance and the promise of belief in Matthew's order: 'If ye have the power of God, deliver yourselves from these bands, and then we will believe.'
provenance.significance: This is the taunt reproduced whole, and the Book of Mormon has made only the substitutions the situation forces: 'the power of God' for 'the King of Israel', 'deliver yourselves from these bands' for 'come down from the cross'. The prior verse of the taunt is present too — Alma 14:20's 'If ye have such great power, why do ye not deliver yourselves?' is Matthew 27:40's 'If thou be the Son of God, come down from the cross', and 14:15's 'ye see that ye had not power to save these which had been cast into the fire' is 27:42's 'He saved others; himself he cannot save'. All three clauses of the crucifixion mockery are in this chapter, in order, spread over ten verses. And the mockers are answered: at 14:25-28 the power of God does arrive, the bands are loosed, and the men who demanded the sign are killed by it. Matthew's taunt is left unanswered on the cross; Alma 14 answers it, which is a reading of Matthew 27:42 as much as a borrowing from it.

14:24.note: 'If ye have the power of God, deliver yourselves from these bands, and then we will believe that the Lord will destroy this people according to your words.' A five-word KJV singleton with the whole shape of the crucifixion mockery around it, and the chapter has already used the taunt's other two clauses at 14:15 and 14:20. Below Skousen's threshold and not among his thirty-six.
14:24.text: He saved others; himself he cannot save. If he be the King of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him.

provenance.other: “the LORD will destroy this” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 19:14: 'Up, get you out of this place; for the LORD will destroy this city. But he seemed as one that mocked unto his sons in law.' Alma 14:24's clause is 'the Lord will destroy this people according to your words', and the words are put in the mouth of a man who is mocking.
provenance.significance: Genesis 19:14 is the KJV's one verse in which a warning of destruction is delivered and TAKEN AS A JOKE, and the Book of Mormon has kept both halves. Lot's sons-in-law think he is mocking; the chief judge of Ammonihah mocks the warning back at the men who gave it, in the same five words. What follows in each case is the same: Sodom is destroyed by fire and Ammonihah is destroyed in Alma 16:9-10, and this chapter has been full of fire since 14:8. The chief judge is telling a prophet what a prophet's warning sounds like to a man who does not believe it, and the sentence he uses to do it is the sentence a man used who was about to be burned.

14:24.note: 'And then we will believe that the Lord will destroy this people according to your words.' A five-word KJV singleton whose one occurrence is a destruction-warning that its hearers found funny. Held at moderate because the phrase is so natural a way to report a prophet's threat that the coincidence could be accidental — but the coincidence includes the mockery and the fire, and the city is destroyed two chapters later.
14:24.whyNot: Five ordinary words in an unremarkable order, and 'the Lord will destroy this people' is the substance of every prophetic warning in the book. The situational match with Genesis 19:14 is what carries the row, and a reader who reads it as coincidence has a fair case.
14:24.text: And Lot went out, and spake unto his sons in law, which married his daughters, and said, Up, get you out of this place; for the LORD will destroy this city. But he seemed as one that mocked unto his sons in law.

provenance.other: “stood upon their feet” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 11:11 — 'the spirit of life from God entered into them, and they stood upon their feet; and great fear fell upon them which saw them.' The nearest relative is Ezekiel 37:10, 'and they lived, and stood up upon their feet', which has the extra preposition. “great fear” occurs in six KJV verses, and Revelation 11:11 is the one that joins it to men standing on their feet. Alma 14:25 reads 'the power of God was upon Alma and Amulek, and they arose and stood upon their feet', and Alma 14:29 reads 'they were struck with great fear'.
provenance.significance: Revelation 11 is the vision of the two witnesses, and Alma 14:25-29 follows it clause by clause. Two prophets who have prophesied against a city are overpowered by it; the city rejoices over them and torments them; then the spirit of life from God enters them and they stand upon their feet, and great fear falls on those who see; and 'the same hour was there a great earthquake, and the tenth part of the city FELL, and in the earthquake were slain of men seven thousand: and the remnant were affrighted' (11:13). The Book of Mormon has two prophets, a mocking city, a rising to the feet under the power of God, an earthquake, a building that falls, everyone inside it slain, and a remnant that runs. What Revelation gives as apocalyptic vision, Alma 14 gives as event — and the two witnesses of Revelation 11 are the only pair of prophets in the KJV to whom this happens, which is why the chapter's two-man ministry matters to the reading. The single word that anchors it is 'their': Revelation's witnesses are two, and its verbs are plural.

14:25.note: 'When the last had spoken unto them, the power of God was upon Alma and Amulek, and they arose and stood upon their feet.' A four-word KJV singleton, and the singleton belongs to the only passage in the Bible where two prophets, killed or overpowered by a hostile city, rise to their feet and are followed by an earthquake that drops a building and kills the onlookers. The sequence runs on through 14:27-29 and the recurrence list carries it. Ezekiel 37:10 is recorded as the alternative for the standing itself; it has no city, no pair, and no earthquake.
14:25.text: And after three days and an half the spirit of life from God entered into them, and they stood upon their feet; and great fear fell upon them which saw them.

provenance.other: “How long, O Lord” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 6:10. The psalter's versions are worded otherwise — Psalm 13:1 'How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD?', Psalm 35:17 'Lord, how long wilt thou look on?', Habakkuk 1:2 'O LORD, how long shall I cry' — so the vocative in exactly this position is the Apocalypse's. Alma 14:26 reads 'How long shall we suffer these great afflictions, O Lord? O Lord, give us strength'.
provenance.significance: Revelation 6:9-10 is the cry of 'the souls of them that were slain for the word of God … and they cried with a loud voice, saying, How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth?' Alma has just watched people burned for the word of God and has told Amulek, at 14:11, that their blood will 'cry mightily against them at the last day' — which is Revelation 6:10's petition in Alma's own words. Fifteen verses later he cries the martyrs' cry himself, in Revelation's exact vocative. The chapter has therefore quoted the same passage twice: once as a prediction about the dead and once as a prayer by the living, and the second is the first coming true early. Alma is granted what the souls under the altar are told to wait for.

14:26.note: 'And Alma cried, saying, How long shall we suffer these great afflictions, O Lord? O Lord, give us strength according to our faith which is in Christ, even unto deliverance.' Four words of a KJV singleton, and the singleton is the cry of martyrs killed for the word of God — which is precisely who has just died in this chapter, and precisely the reading Alma gave of their blood at 14:11.
14:26.text: And they cried with a loud voice, saying, How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth?

provenance.other: Two KJV singletons stand in one verse of Acts. “the foundations of the prison” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “bands were loosed” occurs in exactly one, and they are the same verse, Acts 16:26 — 'And suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken: and immediately all the doors were opened, and every one’s bands were loosed.' Alma 14:27 has 'the earth shook mightily, and the walls of the prison were wrent in twain', and 14:28 has 'they were loosed from their bands'.
provenance.significance: Acts 16 is the New Testament's prison-earthquake and the Book of Mormon has taken the whole episode, not the sentence. Two missionaries are seized by a mob for interfering with the town's business, their clothes are torn off them (16:22, 'they rent off their clothes' — compare Alma 14:22, 'they also did take from them their clothes'), they are beaten, they are put in the inner prison, they pray, an earthquake shakes the prison's foundations, and every bond is loosed; the jailer 'came trembling, and fell down before Paul and Silas' (16:29), as the men of Ammonihah 'fell to the earth' at 14:27. The one change is the outcome, and it is total: in Acts the prison stands, nobody dies, and the jailer is converted; in Alma 14 the prison falls on the men inside it and every soul but the two prisoners is killed. Ammonihah gets Philippi's earthquake without Philippi's mercy, and the chapter has been arguing since 14:11 that this is just.

14:27.note: 'The earth shook mightily, and the walls of the prison were wrent in twain, so that they fell to the earth; and the Chief Judge, and the Lawyers, and Priests, and teachers which smote upon Alma and Amulek, were slain by the fall thereof.' Two KJV singletons from one verse of Acts 16 are distributed across Alma 14:27-28, and the surrounding episode matches at five further points set out in provenance. The 1830 spelling 'wrent' is the first edition's throughout.
14:27.text: And suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken: and immediately all the doors were opened, and every one’s bands were loosed.

provenance.other: “rent in twain” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 27:51 and Mark 15:38, both of the temple veil at the death of Jesus. Matthew's is the one that continues 'and the earth did quake, and the rocks rent', so Matthew 27:51 alone joins a rending in twain to an earthquake — which is the pair Alma 14:27 has: 'the earth shook mightily, and the walls of the prison were wrent in twain'. The 1830 reads 'wrent', an archaic past participle the later editions kept.
provenance.significance: The chapter has been running the passion narrative since 14:14 — the blows on the cheek, the silence before the judge, Pilate's claim of power, the mockers' 'we will believe him' — and this is where it ends, on the two things Matthew reports at the moment of death. What is rent in Matthew is the veil that shut men out of the holy place; what is rent here is the wall that shut two prophets in. The reversal is exact and the Book of Mormon does not comment on it.

14:27.note: 'The walls of the prison were wrent in twain.' One of two KJV verses, and the one of the two that also has the earthquake Alma 14:27 supplies in the same clause. Held at moderate: three words, and the phrase is available English for anything torn in half. The Acts 16:26 row at this verse carries the stronger case and this one sits beside it as the passion chapter's closing echo.
14:27.whyNot: Three words, and the sense in Matthew is a curtain torn from top to bottom by God at the moment of death, not a wall thrown down by an earthquake. If the passion sequence across 14:14-24 is declined, this falls with it.
14:27.text: And, behold, the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom; and the earth did quake, and the rocks rent;
